
### Causal reasoning under random interference {#sec-random-interference .unnumbered}

####

In the previous section we considered interference with a fixed network structure and introduced the simplifying assumption of homogenous network interference. But in many real-world settings, connections themselves are uncertain or vary across time. To capture this type of random interference, we extend our framework to include stochastic network structures.  

#### Random graphs {#sec-random-graphs}

Random graphs bring probability into the network itself. Instead of assuming we know exactly which edges exist, we treat them as random variables. In [Example 3](#sec-example-3), for instance, every week the townspeople possibly change their community of residence and/or the communities they visit. Random graph allows us to model a time-varying pattern of interference, or even different patterns of interference for different variables. 

#### Homogeneous random interference {#sec-homogeneous-random}

We assume that homogenous interference holds, given a set of random draws from the random graph models included.This mirrors the homogeneous assumption from the fixed network setting, but now exposures vary both with treatment assignments and with the random realization of the network.  

#### Bipartite graphs {#sec-bipartite-graphs}

A bipartite graph is one where nodes are divided into two disjoint sets and edges connect only across sets. In random interference problems, it is often useful to model people on one side and places or events on the other. An edge then represents a persons affiliation with a place, and interference arises because multiple people may be connected through the same location. This structure allows us to represent exposures that are not purely person-to-person, but mediated by shared environments.
